strengths: Addresses a timely and relevant problem: scalable, history-aware routing over large MCP tool/agent candidate spaces, which is a genuine bottleneck for the emerging 'Agent Web' setting.

The training pipeline is clearly motivated and well-structured: graph-based candidate expansion via mutation operators, random-walk-based subset sampling, multi-agent trajectory synthesis, and a lightweight plug-and-play routing agent with a minimal two-tool interface.

Evaluation covers real-world benchmarks (MCP-Universe, MCP-Mark) and a broad set of baselines (embedding retrievers, ReAct agents, and many LLM routers), with multiple input settings (query-only vs. query+history).

Useful analyses beyond the main table: scalability to merged multi-server tool pools, robustness to external noise and hard negatives, cross-domain transfer to agent routing, and an ablation isolating the contribution of historical context (53%->48%, 60%->52%).

The history-aware supervision formulation (transforming multi-step trajectories into routing instances with H as context) is a clean and reusable contribution, and implementation details (LoRA rank, LR schedule, seq length, avg@5) are reported.
weaknesses: Circularity in the robustness evaluation: the '+Mutation' distractors are generated by the exact same self-evolutionary mutation mechanism used to create training data, so the near-zero degradation (53.44->53.02) may simply reflect that the router was trained on this synthetic distribution rather than genuine robustness to unseen noise.

Potential train/test contamination and label-quality concerns: trajectory synthesis mutates and simulates tools in the same stylistic space as evaluation candidates, and supervision labels come from GPT-4o-simulated (environment-free) tool results with no reported verification of trajectory correctness or human validation, so the router may learn GPT-4o's preferences rather than ground-truth routing.

Evaluation protocol is under-specified: it is unclear whether reported 'accuracy' is step-level routing accuracy or end-to-end task success, how ground-truth routes on MCP-Universe/MCP-Mark were established, and how candidate spaces were constructed at eval time; only the 'easy mode' of MCP-Mark is used; no confidence intervals or significance tests, and MCP-Mark per-environment numbers (10-100%) suggest very small sample sizes.

The agent-routing generalization claim rests on only 156 self-constructed test samples generated by the authors' own mutation mechanism, making the 91.6% figure weak evidence for 'universal dispatch' in an open Agent Web.

Missing comparisons to trained/tool-retrieval baselines that directly target this problem (e.g., fine-tuned retrievers on tool-retrieval datasets, ToolNet/AutoTool-style graph methods, or RAG-MCP), so it is hard to attribute gains to history-awareness vs. any supervised fine-tuning.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or data release is mentioned; the dataset construction, multi-agent simulation setup (planner/assistant/user/tool agent prompts beyond two mutation prompts), and agent bank normalization details are insufficient to replicate.

Several presentation and scholarship issues: duplicated reference entries (Guo et al. 2025b/c; Lin et al. 2025a/b), inconsistent claims (Robustness section quotes 56.00% under +LiveMCP while Table 2 lists 56.00 vs. text elsewhere), and no ablation of the mutation/graph components themselves.

strengths: The problem is timely and relevant to NLP/agents: tool and agent routing at MCP scale is a genuine bottleneck for open agent ecosystems, and a dedicated history-aware router is a reasonable solution direction.

The evaluation covers a diverse set of baselines: embedding-based retrieval (two encoders, query-only and query+history), a ReAct agent, and many LLM-based routers including strong closed models (GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-Sonnet-4), with downstream execution fixed to a single model for fairer comparison.

The design of the robustness analysis (multi-server merged pools, +Mutation hard negatives, +LiveMCP real external tools) and the history ablation (53%→48% on MCP-Universe, 60%→52% on MCP-Mark) are meaningful experiments that partially support the history-awareness claim.
Implementation details (LoRA config, hyperparameters, avg@5 with temperature 1) and prompts for mutation/synthesis are provided in the appendix, aiding some reproducibility.
weaknesses: Potential train/test contamination undermines the headline results: the training tool bank is built directly from MCP-Universe and LiveMCP tools, and the router is then evaluated on MCP-Universe and MCP-Mark with no explicit decontamination analysis. Worse, the '+Mutation' robustness distractors are generated by the exact same Self-Evolutionary mutation process used to create training data, so the router was effectively trained on the very distractor distribution it is praised for resisting. The robustness claims are therefore circular.

The router is fine-tuned (LoRA on Qwen3-8B) while all baselines are evaluated zero-shot. There is no matched control, e.g., the same backbone fine-tuned on flat query-tool pairs or on ToolACE-style data, so it is impossible to isolate whether gains come from history-awareness, graph-based expansion, or simply fine-tuning. The only component-level ablation is the history ablation; the graph construction, mutation operators, and random-walk sampling are never ablated, and the threshold τ=0.82 receives no sensitivity analysis.

The generalization claims are weakly supported. The Agent Route Benchmark is self-constructed with only 156 samples, generated by the same synthesis pipeline as the training data (circularity risk), and baseline results are presented only in a radar chart (Figure 3) without numeric values, making the claimed superiority (91.6% vs. baselines) unverifiable from the paper.

Scalability claims are overstated relative to evidence. The largest candidate pool is ~2,005 tools; statements about 'massive candidate spaces', 'web-scale open tool ecosystems', and serving as 'foundational infrastructure' for an Agent Web of millions of agents are speculation, not demonstrated. Figure 1 advertises 'Strong Scaling Ability' that the experiments do not establish.

Test sets are small with coarse granularity: MCP-Mark results move in 10-point increments (suggesting ~10-50 samples per domain), and no statistical significance testing is reported for the avg@5 results, despite several margins being modest (e.g., 53.44% vs. 49.79%).
Ground-truth routing labels come entirely from LLM-simulated trajectories with no human verification or quality audit, so label noise in the 15,092 training samples is unquantified.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code, data, or model release is mentioned; the graph construction, trajectory synthesis, and router input formats are described only at a high level in the main text.

Presentation issues: the reference list contains duplicated entries (e.g., Lin et al. 2025a/2025b and Guo et al. 2025b/2025c are identical), and the writing leans on inflated rhetoric ('Agent Web', 'universal dispatcher') rather than precise claims.

strengths: Timely and relevant problem: history-aware routing over large MCP tool/agent spaces is directly aligned with current NLP/agent research, and the paper clearly motivates why static injection and embedding-based retrieval fall short.

The pipeline is well structured and clearly described: graph-based candidate expansion via mutation operators, random-walk subset sampling, LLM-simulated multi-turn trajectory synthesis, and a lightweight plug-and-play routing agent with a minimal two-tool interface.

Comparatively broad evaluation: real-world benchmarks (MCP-Universe, MCP-Mark), diverse baselines spanning embedding retrieval, ReAct agents, and many LLM routers (Qwen3-8B, GPT-4o/4.1, Gemini-2.5-Pro/Flash, Claude, DeepSeek, GLM), with fixed downstream execution model for fairness and avg@5 reporting.

Useful ablation and analysis: the history-removal ablation (53%→48%, 60%→52%) directly supports the central 'history-aware' claim, and the scalability/noise-robustness experiments probe practical deployment concerns.

The tool-to-agent transfer experiment (91.6% on agent routing without agent-specific training) is an interesting finding if it holds, and the mutation taxonomies and prompts in the appendices provide reasonable implementation transparency.
Generally clear writing, with an honest Limitations section acknowledging the LoRA/Qwen3-8B constraint and tool-only training.
weaknesses: Potential train/evaluation overlap is not addressed: the 627-tool initial bank is collected from MCP-Universe and LiveMCP, and the router is then evaluated on MCP-Universe. The paper never states whether the evaluation candidate spaces contain tools seen during training (with mutated variants and synthesized trajectories over them). If so, the headline claim of beating GPT-4o and Gemini-2.5-Pro may partly reflect familiarity with the exact tool descriptions rather than superior routing ability. This must be explicitly clarified or disentangled (e.g., evaluation on held-out tools/servers).

The robustness-against-+Mutation result is somewhat circular: mutation-generated distractors are a core part of training supervision, so the router's stability under the +Mutation setting is largely by design rather than an emergent generalization property, which the text over-claims.

Statistical rigor is thin: MCP-Mark results move in 2% increments (implying ~50 samples), the self-constructed Agent Route Benchmark has only 156 samples, and no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported despite avg@5 being available; several per-domain wins look small relative to this granularity.

Reproducibility is uncertain: no stated release of code, data, or the synthesized 15k-sample dataset; given that GPT-4o-simulated trajectories and mutation operators are the core contribution, absence of an artifact release limits verification.

The 'generalization to the Agent Web' narrative rests on a 156-sample, self-built agent benchmark created with the same mutation/trajectory machinery as the training pipeline, and the paper's Agent Web framing is more aspirational than substantiated.

Benchmark score patterns are suspicious in places (e.g., many baselines at exactly round values like 20.00/30.00/100.00 on MCP-Mark), and the evaluation protocol for how candidate spaces are constructed per test instance is under-specified.
Bibliography quality issues (duplicate entries, e.g., Guo et al. 2025b/c, Lin et al. 2025a/b; inconsistent venues) and some imprecise wording suggest the manuscript needed another editing pass.

Missing ablations on design choices that would strengthen soundness: effect of the similarity threshold (τ=0.82), graph sampling strategy, number of mutation rounds, and router scale/LoRA rank are unexplored, so the contribution of individual components is not isolated beyond the history ablation.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant problem: history-aware tool/agent routing for large-scale MCP ecosystems, with a clearly motivated gap (static injection vs. embedding-based retrieval).

The training pipeline is well-motivated and coherently designed: graph-based candidate expansion via self-evolutionary mutation, random-walk subset sampling, multi-agent trajectory synthesis, and a minimal Light Routing Agent interface that decouples routing from execution.

Empirical evaluation covers two real-world benchmarks (MCP-Universe, MCP-Mark) with a broad set of baselines spanning embedding retrieval, ReAct agents, and multiple LLM routers, plus a downstream execution model held fixed for fairness.

Ablations are targeted and informative: removing history (53%→48%, 60%→52%), removing mutation, and a vanilla fine-tuning variant each isolate a component's contribution, and stronger sparse/dense retrievers (BM25, Contriever, Qwen3-Embedding-8B) are added in the appendix.

The appendix reports standard deviations over 5 runs, includes a human validation of synthesized supervision labels (Cohen's κ = 0.93 on 100 sampled trajectories), and provides full prompts and mutation taxonomies, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Evaluation sets are small, making headline gains fragile: the self-built Agent Route Benchmark has only 156 samples, MCP-Mark per-environment cells appear to rest on ~10 tasks (a 10-point change = 3 tasks), and per-domain MCP-Universe cells are similarly coarse. Despite reporting STDs, no significance tests are provided, and several per-domain margins are within noise.

Potential train/test contamination is not addressed: training tools are drawn from MCP Universe and LiveMCP servers, and mutations are applied to those tools; the paper does not verify that the trained router never saw mutated variants or near-duplicates of the exact benchmark tool spaces it is later evaluated on, which could inflate the +Mutation robustness results.

Scalability claims are overstated relative to evidence: the candidate space is ~2,005 tools, and it is unclear how the router (a generative 8B model) scores a large candidate set at inference (e.g., whether all candidates sit in the context), which bears directly on the 'web-scale Agent Web' framing that the experiments cannot support.

The cross-domain 'generalization to agent routing' claim rests entirely on a self-constructed benchmark with ambiguous ground truth and unclear baseline prompting (e.g., whether LLM routers receive identical history and candidate-specification formats), weakening a central selling point.

Novelty is moderate: the components (self-evolutionary tool synthesis, trajectory synthesis, tool graphs) are combinations of existing ideas (ToolACE, Toolflow, ToolNet, AlphaEvolve-style mutation), and the paper does not clearly delineate its contribution beyond integration.

Presentation and citation hygiene issues: several references carry implausible identifiers (arXiv:2512.x, arXiv:2601.x), cross-references to 'Table 9' appear before it exists, minor grammatical errors occur throughout, and only MCP-Mark 'easy mode' is used without justification.

The abstract states code availability with an empty URL, and key implementation details (candidate-set construction at inference, how LLM baselines ingest history) are underspecified for reproduction.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant problem: history-aware tool/agent routing in the MCP era, which fits squarely within current NLP/agent research interests.

The evaluation covers a reasonably broad set of baselines: embedding retrievers (query-only and query+history variants), a ReAct agent, and a dozen LLM routers including strong closed-source models, with standard deviations over 5 runs reported in the appendix.

Ablation studies (w/o history, w/o mutation, vanilla fine-tuning) are provided and support the claimed contribution of each component, and a human evaluation of the synthesized labels (Cohen's kappa of 0.93 on 100 sampled trajectories) adds some credibility to the supervision quality.

The Light Routing Agent abstraction (routing decoupled from execution via a minimal two-tool interface) is a sensible engineering design, and the fixed downstream execution model across router-based methods is a fair experimental control.
The paper is generally well organized, and the pipeline (graph construction, mutation, trajectory synthesis, SFT) is described in enough procedural detail (with prompts in the appendix) to follow.
weaknesses: Potential train/test contamination undermines the central claims. The training tool bank is built by mutating tools drawn from MCP-Universe and LiveMCP, and evaluation is then conducted on MCP-Universe (and MCP-Mark, whose provenance relative to the training data is not clearly delineated). Training on semantically similar mutations of the very benchmark tools being evaluated risks the router effectively memorizing the target candidates, which is never addressed or ruled out.

The robustness claim is partly circular. The +Mutation noise setting injects distractors generated by the same Self-Evolutionary synthesis pipeline used to create training data, so 'robustness' under this setting is largely in-distribution rather than evidence of genuine resistance to unseen noise. This is not discussed.

Missing comparison against the closest prior art. Baselines are zero-shot LLMs and embedding retrievers; no head-to-head against specialized trained routers or closely related graph/trajectory-synthesis methods (e.g., ToolFlow, ToolNet, ToolACE-style synthesis, AutoTool). Without these, the delta of the proposed pipeline over existing data-synthesis-for-routing recipes is unclear and the novelty claim is weakened.

Statistical support is thin relative to the claims. MCP-Mark appears to contain ~50 samples (accuracy deltas of 2% correspond to single tasks), yet headline differences (e.g., 60.00 vs 48.00; 91.67% vs 88.46% on the 156-sample agent benchmark) are reported without significance testing; the appendix claims 'statistically significant improvements' but only reports standard deviations.

The generalization result (agent routing at 91.6% with no agent-domain training) is based on a small, self-constructed 156-sample test set built by the same mutation machinery as the training data, and Figure 3 lacks variance reporting; the 3-point margin over the best baseline may not be meaningful.

Overclaiming relative to evidence: the router is evaluated with roughly 2,000 tools, yet the paper repeatedly frames results as validating 'web-scale' ecosystems and universal orchestration for the 'Agent Web.' The scalability analysis is a modest merged-pool setting, not a massive-space experiment.

End-to-end benchmark scores conflate routing quality with downstream execution quality (fixed Gemini-2.5-Pro executor), and the paper does not report router-only metrics on held-out routing instances, which would more directly validate the router itself.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the code link is empty ('available at' with no URL), the 'over 15,092 training samples' phrasing is imprecise, the method text confusingly alternates between 'random walk' and 'DFS-style' traversal without precise sampling parameters, and the embedding-baseline Q+H encoding scheme is underspecified.
Only 'easy mode' of MCP-Mark is used, and results on MCP-Mark are sparse-grained, both of which limit the strength of the robustness conclusions.

strengths: Timely and relevant problem: history-aware tool/agent routing for large-scale MCP-style ecosystems directly addresses scalability and generality bottlenecks that are well-documented in recent tool-learning literature, and the framing (static injection vs. embedding retrieval vs. learned router) is clearly motivated by Figure 1.

The training pipeline is well specified end-to-end: graph construction with an explicit similarity threshold, a taxonomy of mutation operators (Appendix C), random-walk subset sampling, multi-turn trajectory synthesis, and a minimal two-tool Light Routing Agent interface. This is more concrete than much of the tool-selection literature.

Evaluation is comparatively thorough for this area: two public benchmarks (MCP-Universe, MCP-Mark), diverse baselines spanning embedding retrievers (including stronger BM25/Contriever/Qwen3-Embedding-8B variants in Appendix A), ReAct agents, and many strong LLM routers; four robustness/scalability settings; ablations isolating history, mutation, and vanilla fine-tuning; standard deviations over 5 runs (Tables 8-9); and human verification of synthetic labels (Cohen's kappa = 0.93, Appendix B).

The history ablation (53% vs 48% MCP-Universe; 60% vs 52% MCP-Mark) and the mutation ablation (53.44/60.00 vs 47.12/44.00 vs 46.70/42.00) support the paper's core claims that both history-awareness and hard-negative synthesis contribute meaningfully rather than the gains coming from fine-tuning alone.
Reproducibility posture is reasonable: LoRA hyperparameters, embedding models, training data sizes, prompts (Appendix E), and a stated code release are provided.
weaknesses: Potential train/test overlap is not adequately analyzed. The training tool bank is built from MCP-Universe and LiveMCP tools, and evaluation is then performed on MCP-Universe and MCP-Mark. Queries may be unseen, but the router has trained extensively on exactly these tools (and their mutation variants); the paper should explicitly discuss and quantify this overlap and its effect on reported generalization.

The Agent Route Benchmark (the basis for the headline 91.6% generalization result) is small (156 samples) and self-constructed using the same self-evolutionary mutation machinery used in training. The claim of cross-domain 'capability matching' transfer is therefore partly circular; performance on an independently constructed agent-routing benchmark would substantially strengthen the claim.

The strongest-competitor margins are modest in places. On MCP-Universe, ACE-Router's 53.44 vs. Gemini-2.5-Pro's 49.79 is within a few points, and per-domain results are mixed; no significance tests are reported despite the variance data. Figure 3's truncated y-axis (75-95) visually exaggerates agent-benchmark differences.

Key inference details are underspecified: how the candidate space is surfaced to the router at inference (how many candidates, how tool specs are serialized into context), how history is formatted, and how the Q+H embedding baselines encode history. This limits the ability to reproduce or interpret the scalability results.

Methodological novelty is moderate: the pipeline combines known ingredients (LLM-based tool synthesis as in ToolACE/ToolFlow, graph-based tool organization as in ToolNet/ToolChain, LoRA fine-tuning). The contribution is largely an empirical/systems integration rather than a new technique, which should be stated more explicitly.

Simulated, environment-free trajectory generation (GPT-4o simulating tool outputs) may teach the router spurious correlations with simulated rather than real execution feedback; the kappa study on 100 samples is reassuring for labels but does not test distribution shift of the simulated responses themselves.

Presentation issues: the abstract's code-availability sentence is truncated/incomplete, Figure 2 is cluttered, there are typos ('toolgraph', 'candidate space.Based'), and temperature=1 with avg@5 is an unusual choice that is not justified.
